# Stencil patterns for the library's shelf labels

The library's label printer selects labels with stencils. `stencil(pattern, text)` tests whether a whole text fits a pattern written in the house stencil notation.

## Notation

The pattern must match the **whole** text, not just a part of it. Text and pattern are ASCII. Every character of the pattern matches itself, except these:

* `?` matches any single character.
* `*` matches any run of characters, possibly empty (a *lazy* run: see *Order of attempts*).
* `\` followed by any character matches that character literally (so `\\` matches a backslash and `\*` a literal `*`). A `\` at the very end of the pattern is an error.

## Order of attempts

When there are several ways to match, the first one found in this order is used (this only matters for the captures below): wildcards and alternatives are tried left to right; a `*` tries the shortest run first; the choices of earlier parts are changed last.

## Result

`yes` if the text fits, `no` if not.

## Errors

A bad pattern gives `error: pattern at I: WHY` (instead of `yes`/`no`, whatever the text is). `I` is a position in the pattern counting from 1 and `WHY` one of:

* `escape`: a `\` at the end of the pattern (`I` is its position).

The pattern is read once from left to right and the **first** problem found is reported.

## Interface

Implement this function in `src/stencil.c`; the declaration is already in `include/stencil.h`. The returned string is allocated with `malloc` and the caller frees it:

```
char *stencil(const char *pattern, const char *text)
```

* `pattern`: the pattern
* `text`: the text to test
* returns `no`, `yes` (with captures) or an error text.

All inputs and the result are plain strings. Invalid input is reported *inside the result text* as the rules in this document say; the function itself never throws, panics or exits.

## Examples

| pattern | text | result |
|---|---|---|
| `ab*ef` | `abcdef` | `yes` |
| `?at*` | `cattle` | `yes` |
| `a?c` | `ac` | `no` |

Run the visible tests with `mkdir -p build && gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Iinclude -Isrc -o build/tests $(find src tests -name '*.c') && ./build/tests`.

# Stencil patterns for the lighthouse log filter

The lighthouse log viewer selects entries with stencils. `stencil(pattern, text)` tests whether a whole text fits a pattern written in the house stencil notation.

## Notation

The pattern must match the **whole** text, not just a part of it. Text and pattern are ASCII. Every character of the pattern matches itself, except these:

* `?` matches any single character.
* `%` matches any run of characters, possibly empty (a *lazy* run: see *Order of attempts*).
* `\` followed by any character matches that character literally (so `\\` matches a backslash and `\%` a literal `%`). A `\` at the very end of the pattern is an error.
* a ``` as the **first** character of the pattern switches on case-insensitive matching for the whole pattern and matches nothing itself (anywhere else it is an ordinary character).
* `[...]` is a character class matching one character. Inside: items are single characters or ranges `x-y` (both ends included, `x` must not be greater than `y` in ASCII order). A `^` right after the `[` negates the class. A `]` that is the first item (right after `[` or `[^`) is a literal `]`; otherwise `]` ends the class. A `-` is a range operator only between two items (a range needs a character after the `-` that is not the closing `]`), so `-` first or last is literal. `\` inside a class makes the next character literal (also as a range end, as in `[a-\]]`). Other characters, including `[`, are literal. A class that never closes is an error.

With the case flag, two characters are equal if they are equal after turning ASCII capitals into lower case. A class then matches a character if the class contains it **or** contains its other-case counterpart (before negation: `[^a]` with the flag rejects both `a` and `A`).

## Order of attempts

When there are several ways to match, the first one found in this order is used (this only matters for the captures below): wildcards and alternatives are tried left to right; a `%` tries the shortest run first; the choices of earlier parts are changed last.

## Result

`yes` if the text fits, `no` if not.

## Errors

A bad pattern gives `error: pattern at I: WHY` (instead of `yes`/`no`, whatever the text is). `I` is a position in the pattern counting from 1 and `WHY` one of:

* `escape`: a `\` at the end of the pattern (`I` is its position).
* `class`: a `[` that is never closed (`I` is the position of the `[`). A `\` at the very end of the pattern inside a class is also reported as `class`.
* `range`: a range whose start is greater than its end (`I` is the position of the start of the range; if the start is written `\x`, the position of the `\`).

The pattern is read once from left to right and the **first** problem found is reported.

## Interface

Implement this function in `src/lib.rs` (library crate `stencil`):

```
pub fn stencil(pattern: &str, text: &str) -> String
```

* `pattern`: the pattern
* `text`: the text to test
* returns `no`, `yes` (with captures) or an error text.

All inputs and the result are plain strings. Invalid input is reported *inside the result text* as the rules in this document say; the function itself never throws, panics or exits.

## Examples

| pattern | text | result |
|---|---|---|
| `ab%ef` | `abcdef` | `yes` |
| `?at%` | `cattle` | `yes` |
| `a?c` | `ac` | `no` |
| ``stop%` | `STOPPING` | `yes` |
| `[a-c]?[^0-9]` | `b2x` | `yes` |

import os
import sys
import unittest

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "src"))
from stencil import stencil  # noqa: E402

CASES = [
    (("ab*ef", "abcdef"), "yes"),
    (("?at*", "cattle"), "yes"),
    (("a?c", "ac"), "no"),
    (("~stop*", "STOPPING"), "yes"),
    (("[a-c]?[!0-9]", "b2x"), "yes"),
]


class Cases(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_cases(self):
        for args, want in CASES:
            with self.subTest(args=args):
                self.assertEqual(stencil(*args), want)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

A `!` right after the `[` negates the class. A `]` that is the first item (right after `[` or `[!`) is a literal `]`; otherwise `]` ends the class. A `-` is a range operator only between two items (a range needs a character after the `-` that is not the closing `]`), so `-` first or last is literal. `\` inside a class makes the next character literal (also as a range end, as in `[a-\]]`). Other characters, including `[`, are literal. A class that never closes is an error.
* `<` starts a group and `>` ends it; inside, alternatives are separated by `,` (outside groups `,` is an ordinary character). A group matches the text matched by any one of its alternatives; an alternative may be empty and groups may be nested. An unmatched `>` or a `<` that is never closed is an error.
* `#` matches any run of characters, possibly empty, like `*`, but is *greedy* (longest run first).
* `&` followed by a digit `1` to `9` is a back-reference: it matches exactly the text that capture number N matched (see *Captures*); with case-insensitive matching the comparison ignores case. A reference to a capture that has not been *completed* earlier in the pattern (or `&` without a digit 1 to 9) is an error. If the referenced capture did not take part in the match, the reference fails to match.

With the case flag, two characters are equal if they are equal after turning ASCII capitals into lower case. A class then matches a character if the class contains it **or** contains its other-case counterpart (before negation: `[!a]` with the flag rejects both `a` and `A`).

## Order of attempts

When there are several ways to match, the first one found in this order is used (this only matters for the captures below): wildcards and alternatives are tried left to right; a `*` tries the shortest run first and a `#` the longest run first; the alternatives of a group are tried in the order written; the choices of earlier parts are changed last.

## Captures

The captures are every `_`, every `*`, every class, every `#`, every group, numbered from 1 in the order in which they **start** in the pattern (a group is numbered before the captures inside it). A capture holds the text it matched in the successful attempt; one that did not take part in the match (for example inside an alternative that was not used) is empty. Escaped characters and plain characters are not captures.

## Result

`no` if the text does not fit; otherwise `yes` followed by one ` [TEXT]` for every capture in order (a space, `[`, the captured text, `]`), for example `yes [b] [] [xy]`. A pattern without captures gives just `yes`.

## Errors

A bad pattern gives `error: pattern at I: WHY` (instead of `yes`/`no`, whatever the text is). `I` is a position in the pattern counting from 1 and `WHY` one of:

* `escape`: a `\` at the end of the pattern (`I` is its position).
* `class`: a `[` that is never closed (`I` is the position of the `[`). A `\` at the very end of the pattern inside a class is also reported as `class`.
* `range`: a range whose start is greater than its end (`I` is the position of the start of the range; if the start is written `\x`, the position of the `\`).
* `group`: an unmatched `>` (`I` is its position) or a `<` that is never closed (`I` is the position of that `<`).
* `reference`: a bad back-reference (`I` is the position of the `&`).

The pattern is read once from left to right and the **first** problem found is reported. A group that is never closed is only noticed at the end of the pattern, so problems after its `<`, if any, are reported first.

## Interface

Implement this function in `src/lib.rs` (library crate `stencil`):

```
pub fn stencil(pattern: &str, text: &str) -> String
```

* `pattern`: the pattern
* `text`: the text to test
* returns `no`, `yes` (with captures) or an error text.

All inputs and the result are plain strings. Invalid input is reported *inside the result text* as the rules in this document say; the function itself never throws, panics or exits.

## Examples

| pattern | text | result |
|---|---|---|
| `ab*ef` | `abcdef` | `yes [cd]` |
| `_at*` | `cattle` | `yes [c] [tle]` |
| `a_c` | `ac` | `no` |
| `~stop*` | `STOPPING` | `yes [PING]` |
| `[a-c]_[!0-9]` | `b2x` | `yes [b] [2] [x]` |
| `<cat,dog>*` | `dogs` | `yes [dog] [s]` |
| `<*>&1` | `abab` | `yes [ab] [ab]` |
